title: History Taking and Pain Assessment
lead: The interview gives you most of the diagnosis. Learn to ask, listen and interpret.

book.title: History Taking and Pain Assessment
book.lead: The interview gives you most of the diagnosis. Learn to ask, listen and interpret.

blocks.text: In most musculoskeletal patients, a well-taken history narrows the diagnosis to two or three options before you touch the patient. The physical examination then tests those options. If you start examining without a hypothesis, you will perform many tests, find many "positives" and still not know what is wrong.

blocks.label: TEACHER'S VOICE
body: Think of yourself as a detective, not a test technician. Every question you ask should either support or weaken a specific idea in your head. If you cannot say why you are asking a question, either drop it or find out what it is for.

sections.title: 2.2 The order of the subjective examination

rows: Age, occupation, hand dominance, sport, home situation
Who is likely to have which condition; what function matters
"What is the main problem that brought you here?" in the patient's own words
The patient's priority and your treatment goal
Exact area of each symptom, depth, quality, constant or intermittent, links between areas
Pattern recognition: local, referred, radicular, widespread
General health, red flags, medications, investigations
Barriers to recovery (yellow, blue and black flags)
"What do you want to be able to do again?"

sections.title: 2.3 The body chart, step by step

items: Ask the patient to point with one finger to the worst area. Draw it and mark it "1".
Ask: "Is there anywhere else?" Draw each further area and number it.
For each area record: quality (ache, sharp, burning, tingling), depth (deep or surface), constant or intermittent, and intensity (0 to 10).
Ask whether the areas are linked: "When area 1 gets worse, does area 2 get worse too?" Linked areas suggest one source.
Check and mark clear areas with a tick, for example "lumbar spine and both legs checked: clear". A clear area is a finding too.

rows: Pain in one joint area, sharp with movement
Deep, vague ache spreading into a limb, no clear border, no neurological change
Sharp, shooting or burning narrow band down a limb, often with tingling
Glove or stocking numbness in both feet or hands
Widespread pain in many regions with sensitivity to light touch
Pain-science based assessment; screen medical causes first

blocks.label: COMMON STUDENT TRAP
body: Students often write "pain in the leg". This is useless. Write "deep ache posterior thigh to knee, intermittent, 6/10, linked to back pain, no paraesthesia". Precision on the body chart saves time in the examination.

blocks.text: Irritability tells you how easily symptoms are provoked and how long they take to settle. It decides how vigorous your examination and treatment can be.

rows: How little activity provokes the pain?
Very little (for example 2 minutes of standing)
How severe is it when provoked?
Hours, or into the next day
Few movements, stop at first pain, no overpressure
Full range, overpressure, combined movements, repeated tests

blocks.text: The SINSS framework adds two more ideas: **Severity**, **Irritability**, **Nature** (the type of condition, including red flags), **Stage** (acute, subacute, persistent) and **Stability** (getting better, worse or staying the same) [Ref – to verify].

blocks.label: TEACHER'S VOICE
body: Write one decision sentence after you judge irritability: "Because symptoms are provoked by 5 minutes of sitting and take 2 hours to settle, I will limit active movements to one repetition each and avoid overpressure today."

rows: Morning stiffness less than about 30 minutes that eases with movement
Morning stiffness more than about an hour, improving with activity, with swelling in several joints
Worse as the day goes on with use
Wakes with pain on rolling but settles on changing position
Constant night pain not affected by position, with sweats or weight loss
Possible serious pathology. Act on red flag guidance
"0 is no pain, 10 is the worst pain imaginable. What is your pain now, at best and at worst in the last 24 hours?"
Patient marks a point on a 10 cm line; measure in mm
Research and patients who prefer a visual scale
Children and some patients with language barriers
Burning, electric, pins and needles, numbness
Screening for neuropathic pain; consider a validated questionnaire [Ref – to verify]

blocks.text: Record three numbers (now, best, worst) rather than one. A change from "worst 8/10" to "worst 5/10" is often more meaningful to the patient than a change in the current rating.

items: **Nociceptive pain**: tissue is being loaded or injured and nerve endings send danger signals. Pain is usually local, proportional to load, and has clear aggravating and easing factors.
**Neuropathic pain**: the nerve itself is injured or diseased. Pain is burning, shooting or electric, follows a nerve or root area, and often comes with numbness or tingling.
**Nociplastic pain (sensitisation)**: the nervous system has become more sensitive. Pain is widespread, disproportionate to the tissue findings, and linked with fatigue, poor sleep and distress.

blocks.text: Most patients have a mix. The dominant mechanism guides your emphasis: tissue loading for nociceptive, nerve-focused care for neuropathic, and education plus graded activity for nociplastic pain.

rows: Beliefs, emotions and behaviours that may slow recovery
"What do you think is causing your pain?" "Are you avoiding anything because you fear it will damage you?"
Perceptions about work that may slow recovery
"How do you feel about returning to work?"
System or contextual obstacles (compensation, policy, family)
"Is anything at work or at home making recovery harder?"
Possible psychiatric disorder needing specialist care
Severe depression, suicidal thoughts: refer through the appropriate pathway

blocks.label: STOP AND THINK
body: If a patient discloses thoughts of self-harm, stop the routine assessment. Respond with care, follow your clinic's safety protocol and arrange appropriate help. This is part of your professional duty, not outside it.

blocks.label: CLINICAL CASE
body: A 38-year-old teacher reports a 3-week history of right buttock pain spreading to the back of the knee. It is a deep ache, 6/10 at worst, worse after 20 minutes of sitting and easing within 10 minutes of walking. No tingling, no weakness, no night pain, no general health problems.

items: **Is this radicular pain?** Probably not. It is a deep ache without a narrow band, tingling or neurological change. It fits somatic referred pain more than radicular pain.
**Is irritability high or low?** Moderate to low: provoked by 20 minutes, settles in 10 minutes. A full active examination is safe.
**What will you examine first?** The lumbar spine and hip, as the likely sources of referred pain.
**Which finding would change your plan?** New tingling below the knee, weakness or reflex change would make you perform a full neurological examination and consider radiculopathy.
**Why record "best" pain too?** It shows whether the patient has pain-free periods, which supports a mechanical, modifiable problem.

sections.title: Now You Should Be Able To

items: Take a structured history in the correct order.
Draw and interpret a precise body chart.
Judge irritability and adjust the examination accordingly.
Distinguish nociceptive, neuropathic and nociplastic pain patterns.
Screen for psychosocial flags with natural questions.
